Vineet Shaky S/o Sh.Keshav Shaky (hereinafter referred as claimant) on account of injuries sustained by him in a road accident which took place on 29.09.2017 due to rash and negligent driving of Truck bearing Registration No. RJ 11 GA 0795 (hereinafter referred as the offending vehicle) which was being driven by Sh. Amir (hereinafter referred as driver/R1),
owned by Sh. Tamjid Khan (hereinafter referred as owner/ R2) and insured with M/s The Oriental Insurance Company Ltd. (hereinafter referred as insurance company/R3). 
2. In the accident in question, claimant sustained grievous injuries while two other persons died at the spot. Accordingly, three separate Claim Petitions were filed before this Tribunal. Present Claim Petition is relating to injuries sustained by the claimant in such alleged road accident. 
MACT No .348/2018 Vineet Shaky vs. Amir Page N  3. Briefly, the facts, as stated in the Claim Petition, are that on 29.09.2017 at about 12.00 (midnight) claimant alongwith other passengers was traveling in Car (i- 10) bearing Registration No. HR 13K 3831 (hereinafter called the accidental vehicle)
which was being driven by Sh. Ashu Chauhan and when they reached on Dankor/Sikandrabad Road, Crown Plaza, PS Dankor, Gautam Budh Nagar, UP (hereinafter called the spot of accident), their car rammed in stationed offending vehicle covered with black Tripal/cover and abandoned on the road without any sign,
indicator or reflector, as result of which driver of accidental vehicle Sh. Ashu Chauhan and Sh.Sunil Kumar (who was sitting beside the driver seat) died at the spot, while claimant (who was sitting on the rear seat of the said car) sustained grievous injuries. It is stated that claimant was rushed to Yatharth Hospital, Greater Noida and then remained hospitalised in Beg Hospital and Fahmy Maternity Centre Bareilly for treatment. It is alleged that accident occurred due to unattended offending vehicle parked in the middle of the road. Further, as per record, FIR No. 0586/2017 was registered at PS Dankor, District Gautam Budh Nagar, UP. After completion of investigation, respondent no.1 was charge-sheeted for commission of offence punishable under Section 279/338/304A IPC.
4. It is further asserted that claimant was employed as Salesman with Paramount Road Safety Equipment Pvt. Ltd., Shop No. 20, 26 & 27, DLF. Tower-B, Jasola, Delhi and was earning Rs.15,000/- per month. It is further asserted that claimant sustained grievous injuries in accident due to which he has not been able to attend the office and suffered huge financial loss. It is further stated that the offending vehicle was in immediate control of respondent no.1, owned by respondent no.2, while it was MACT No .348/2018 Vineet Shaky vs. Amir Page No. 3 of 27 insured with respondent no.3 and hence, all respondents are jointly and severally liable to pay compensation to the petitioners. Hence, the present petition has been filed with a request to pass an Award in the sum of Rs.20,00,000/- alongwith interest @ 12% p.a. from the date of filing of the petition till its realization in favour of the claimant and against the respondents. 
5. Common written statement was filed by respondent Nos. 1 and 2, wherein it is stated that accident took place on account of negligent driving of claimant. It is also stated that the offending vehicle was duly insured and that the driver was holding a valid driving license and as such, liability,
if any, in terms of claim/compensation is upon the insurance company.

2 6. Respondent No.3 in the written statement/reply filed, asserted that accident took place due to sole carelessness and negligence of the driver of accidental vehicle as he was not cautious with the traffic moving ahead and ended up ramming into a stationary truck. It is contended that accident is attributed to contributory negligence on the part of the driver of the said accidental vehicle citing the manner of accident. 
7. From the pleadings of parties, the following issues were framed vide order dated 07.08.2018:
1) Whether the injured suffered injures in a road traffic accident dated 29.09.2017 involving vehicle bearing no. RJ 11 GA 0975 driven by R1 and owned by R2 and insured with R3 due to rash and negligent driving of R1? OPP. 
MACT No .348/2018 Vineet Shaky vs. Amir Page No. 4 of 27 2) Whether the claimant is entitled to any compensation, if so, to what extent and from whom ?
OPP.
3) Relief. 
8. During the course of proceedings, upon moving an application, claimant was referred to Pt.
Madan Mohan Malviya Hospita, GNCTD, Malviya Nagar, New Delhi for getting the physical disability assessed. Report from the said hospital was received with 'zero' percent disability. 
9. Thereafter, matter was proceeded further for Petitioner Evidence. Claimant appeared as PW1 and tendered his evidentiary affidavit as Ex.PW1/A. Claimant relied upon his Aadhar Card Ex.PW1/1,
Medical Treatment bills Ex.PW1/2 (colly), Medical Treatment Record and Discharge Summary Ex.PW1/3, Payment Receipts Ex.PW1/4 (colly) and Salary-cum-Employment Certificate Ex.PW1/5. 
He was put to cross-examination by counsel for insurance company, however, on one appeared on behalf of R-1 & R-2 to cross-examine him. 
10. PW2 Sh. Nitin Kumar Saxena, Manager of M/s Paramount Road Safety Equipment Pvt. Ltd. was also examined by claimant, who proved his Authority Letter Ex.PW2/1, Appointment Letter of claimant as Ex.PW2/2, Salary Slips from April 2016 to September 2017 as Ex.PW2/3 (18 pages),
Salary Payment Record as Ex.PW2/4 and Certificate under Section 65-B of Evidence Act with respect to computer generated record as Ex.PW2/5.
11. Petitioner's evidence was closed vide order dated 09.09.2022. Matter was then fixed for Respondents Evidence, however, no witness was examined on behalf of MACT No .348/2018 Vineet Shaky vs. Amir Page No. 5 of 27 Respondent Nos. 1 and 2 while insurance company/Respondent No.
3 examined Ms.Lalita Anand as R3W1, who tendered her evidentiary affidavit Ex.R3W1/1 and relied upon documents Ex.R3W1/A to R3W1/E. Thereafter, respondents evidence was closed vide order dated 01.08.2023. 
Vineet Shaky vs Amir on 4 July, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/27361723/
3 12. Final Arguments in detail were addressed by Ld. counsel for claimant and Ld. counsel for insurance company. 
13. Ld. counsel for claimant contended that accident occurred due to negligence of driver of offending vehicle as he abandoned the offending vehicle on the road and that too, covered with black Tripal without any indicator or reflector. He also asserted that claimant sustained serious injuries due to accident and had to incur heavy expenses on his treatment and also suffered income/financial loss. 
14. No one has appeared on behalf of Respondent nos. 1 and 2 to argue on their behalf. 
15. Ld. counsel for insurance company argued that entire case appears to be concocted as the FIR was got lodged after delay of about one month. It is also argued that deceased driver of accidental vehicle was negligent in driving the vehicle, having rammed in a stationary truck ahead. It has also been argued that offending vehicle was not holding a valid fitness certificate. Reliance was placed upon Report Ex.R3W1/B. He stated that Claim Petition deserves to be dismissed. 
16. On the basis of material on record, evidence adduced and arguments addressed, issue wise findings are as under :-
MACT No .348/2018 Vineet Shaky vs. Amir Page No. 6 of 27 Issue No.1 "Whether the injured suffered injuries in a road traffic accident dated 29.09.2017 involving vehicle bearing no. RJ 11 GA 0975 driven by R1 and owned by R2 and insured with R3 due to rash and negligent driving of R1? OPP."
17. What is required to be ascertained is whether there was any breach of duty of care by respondent no.1 towards use of public way, particularly against claimant who allegedly suffered injuries due to his act or omission. It has been held in catena of cases that negligence has to be decided on the touchstone of preponderance of probabilities and a holistic view is to be taken. It has been further held that the proceedings under the Motor Vehicle Act are not akin to the proceedings in a Civil Suit and hence, strict rules of evidence are not applicable (support drawn from the case of Bimla Devi &
Ors vs. Himachal Road Transport Corporation & Ors. [ (2009) 13 SC 530,[ in Kaushnumma Begum and others v/s New India Assurance Company Limited, [2001 ACJ 421 SC[, in National Insurance Co. Ltd. vs. Pushpa Rana cited as [2009 ACJ 287 Del]. 
18. At the outset, it would be appropriate to deal with the contention of Ld. Counsel for insurance company that entire story has been concocted as there is delay of about one month in lodging the FIR and thus, Claim Petition be dismissed. 
19. Accident in question occurred on 29.09.2017. Perusal of Post-Mortem Reports of deceased Ashu Chauhan (driver of accidental vehicle) and other co-passenger Sunil dated 30.09.2017 record names of police officials of PS Dankaur viz. Gurmeet and MACT No .348/2018 Vineet Shaky vs. Amir Page No. 7 of 27 Israr Ahmad. Thus, it is clear that the factum of accident was very well within the knowledge of police officials of PS Dankaur right after the accident, however they did not lodge FIR. 
Vineet Shaky vs Amir on 4 July, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/27361723/ 
4 It is not in dispute that accidental vehicle rammed in to offending vehicle which was stationed in the middle of the road covered with black Tripal. FIR was lodged on 31.10.2017 upon complaint/statement of Smt. Niraj wife of deceased Sunil. No doubt, there is delay of about one month in lodging the FIR, but it is not attributed to claimant as she was under trauma at that time having lost her husband in the accident in question. As already discussed, the accident was well within the knowledge of police officials of PS Dankaur, however they chose not to lodge the FIR for the reasons best known to them and for the inaction on their part, claimant cannot be held responsible. Following observations made by Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in the case of Ravi vs Badrinarayan & Ors., 2011 (4) SCC 693 are relevant in the context and reproduced as such under :
"20. It is well-settled that delay in lodging FIR cannot be a ground to doubt the claimant's case. 
Knowing the Indian conditions as they are, we cannot expect a common man to first rush to the Police Station immediately after an accident. Human nature and family responsibilities occupy the mind of kith and kin to such an extent that they give more importance to get the victim treated rather than to rush to the Police Station. Under such circumstances, they are not expected to act mechanically with promptitude in lodging the FIR with the Police. Delay in lodging the FIR thus,
cannot be the ground to deny justice to the victim. In cases of delay, the courts are required to examine the evidence with a closer scrutiny and in doing so; the contents of the FIR should also be scrutinized more carefully. If court finds that there is no indication of fabrication or it has not been concocted or engineered to implicate innocent persons then, even if there is a delay in lodging the FIR, the claim case cannot be dismissed merely on that ground. 
MACT No .348/2018 Vineet Shaky vs. Amir Page No. 8 of 27 21. The purpose of lodging the FIR in such type of cases is primarily to intimate the police to initiate investigation of criminal offences. Lodging of FIR certainly proves factum of accident so that the victim is able to lodge a case for compensation but delay in doing so cannot be the main ground for rejecting the claim petition. In other words, although lodging of FIR is vital in deciding motor accident claim cases, delay in lodging the same should not be treated as fatal for such proceedings, if claimant has been able to demonstrate satisfactory and cogent reasons for it. There could be variety of reasons in genuine cases for delayed lodgment of FIR. Unless kith and kin of the victim are able to regain a certain level of tranquility of mind and are composed to lodge it, even if, there is delay, the same deserves to be condoned. In such circumstances, the authenticity of the FIR assumes much more significance than delay in lodging thereof supported by cogent reasons." 
20. There is thus no substance in the objection raised by Ld. Counsel for insurance company seeking dismissal of Claim Petition on account of delay in lodging the FIR. 
21. PW1 has affirmed in his affidavit Ex.PW1/A the mode and manner of accident citing total invisibility of stationary abandoned truck in the middle of road. In cross- examination by Ld.
Counsel for insurance company, PW1 has specifically and categorically stated that offending truck was stationed in the middle of the road. In his further cross-examination, PW1 stated that at the time of accident, he was sitting on the middle part of back seat of accidental vehicle which was running at the speed of 30-40 kmph and that, he was conscious post-accident. Public persons Vineet Shaky vs Amir on 4 July, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/27361723/
5 gathered at the spot who rushed and admitted him to Ram Gopal Hospital. No contrary suggestion has been put to the witness by Ld. Counsel for insurance company. He was the only survivor of the accident as two other persons riding in the accidental vehicle died at the spot. As such, he was the best person to depose about the MACT No .348/2018 Vineet Shaky vs. Amir Page No. 9 of 27 accident. Further, in the Mechanical Inspection Report, fresh damages were found at the back side of the offending vehicle and correspondingly on front of accidental vehicle. Impact of accident on accidental vehicle as evident from Mechanical Inspection Report gives an inference that the driver thereof was totally unaware of any vehicle ahead and could not have anticipated or contemplated any vehicle parked as such. Site Plan filed as a part of charge-sheet also support the deposition of PW1 and shows that offending vehicle was parked right in the middle of the road. Any evidence with respect to non-involvement of the offending vehicle or incorrect identification thereof has not been led by any of the respondents. Investigation Report Ex.PW1/3 (colly) also concludes that offending vehicle was stationed abandoned on the road covered with Black Tripal by respondent no.1 in rash and negligent manner as a result of which accident occurred and claimant suffered injuries while two other persons died at the spot. No case has been set up to show that the respondent no.1 was not at wheels of the offending vehicle at the time of accident. There is nothing on record to doubt the veracity of the petitioner or to disbelieve that the version put forth by him with respect to mode and manner of the accident. 
22. Respondent nos. 1 and 2 have not led any evidence to controvert or contradict or to set up any defence against the contention of the claimant. It is settled that if driver of offending vehicle does not enter the witness box, an adverse inference can be drawn against him as observed by Hon'ble Delhi High Court in the case of Cholamandlam Insurance Company Ltd. Vs. Kamlesh, 2009 (3) AD Delhi 310.
23. The manner of accident is such that mere proof of accident speaks volumes of the rashness and carelessness on the part of respondent no.1 in direct control and MACT No .348/2018 Vineet Shaky vs. Amir Page No. 10 of 27 supervision of offending vehicle. No reason had been attempted to be assigned for leaving unattended heavy vehicle late night covered with black Tripal which directly reduced the visibility to zero unless any person reached close enough that it was virtually not possible to prevent the accident. The speed of accidental vehicle has been stated to be average and not excessive. There is no evidence to show that accidental vehicle was being speedily or rashly driven due to which the driver thereof lost control and rammed into stationary vehicle ahead. It does not appear probable that any act or omission on the part of driver of accidental vehicle qua which he was under a legal obligation to exercise duty of care and caution, led to the accident. Therefore, it cannot be held against claimants that that they could have prevented the accident had they not acted negligently. 
24. It is evident that respondents have failed to exercise duty of care expected of a reasonable person under the prevalent circumstances and acted with utter recklessness and indifference towards the possible anticipated consequences. 
25. Having so analyzed the evidence on record, it is held that respondent no.1 acted rashly and negligently in relation to offending vehicle causing accident. Therefore, any contributory negligence Vineet Shaky vs Amir on 4 July, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/27361723/
6 cannot be attributed to the claimant. Accordingly, Issue no.1 is decided in favour of the petitioners and against the respondents. 
Issue No.2 "Whether the claimant is entitled to any compensation, if so, to what extent and from whom ? OPP." 
MACT No .348/2018 Vineet Shaky vs. Amir Page No. 11 of 27 26. Section 168 MV Act enjoins the Claim Tribunals to hold an enquiry into the claim to make an effort determining the amount of compensation which appears to it to be just and reasonable. Same is reproduced hereunder for ready reference:
"(1) Award of the Claims Tribunal.--On receipt of an application for compensation made under section 166 , the Claims Tribunal shall, after giving notice of the application to the insurer and after giving the parties (including the insurer) an opportunity of being heard, hold an inquiry into the claim or, as the case may be,
each of the claims and, subject to the provisions of section 162 may make an award determining the amount of compensation which appears to it to be just and specifying the person or persons to whom compensation shall be paid and in making the award the Claims Tribunal shall specify the amount which shall be paid by the insurer or owner or driver of the vehicle involved in the accident or by all or any of them, as the case may be: Provided that where such application makes a claim for compensation under section 140 in respect of the death or permanent disablement of any person, such claim and any other claim (whether made in such application or otherwise) for compensation in respect of such death or permanent disablement shall be disposed of in accordance with the provisions of Chapter X. (2) The Claims Tribunal shall arrange to deliver copies of the award to the parties concerned expeditiously and in any case within a period of fifteen days from the date of the award.
(3) When an award is made under this section, the person who is required to pay any amount in terms of such award shall, within thirty days of the date of announcing the award by the Claims Tribunal, deposit the entire amount awarded in such manner as the Claims Tribunal may direct." 
27. Before putting in frame the position of law, it is noted that the process of determining the compensation by the court is essentially a very difficult task and can MACT No .348/2018 Vineet Shaky vs. Amir Page No. 12 of 27 never be an exact science. Perfect compensation is hardly possible,
more so in claims of injury and disability. (As observed by Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in the case of Sidram Vs. The Divisional Manager United India Insurance Company Ltd, SLP (Civil) No.
19277 of 2019) . 
28. The basic principle in assessing motor vehicle compensation claims, is to place the victim in as near a position as she or he was in before the accident, with other compensatory directions for loss Vineet Shaky vs Amir on 4 July, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/27361723/
7 of amenities and other payments. These general principles have been stated and reiterated in several decisions. [Support drawn from Govind Ram Yadav vs. New India Insurance Company Ltd., (2011)
10 SCC 683] .
29. This Tribunal has been tasked with determination of just compensation. The observation of Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in Divisional Controller, KSRTC vs. Mahadeva Shetty & Anr.,
(2003) 7 SCC 197, needs mention here (para 15): 
"Statutory provisions clearly indicate that the compensation must be "just" and it cannot be a bonanza; not a source of profit but the same should not be a pittance. The courts and tribunals have a duty to weigh the various factors and quantify the amount of compensation, which should be just. What would be "just" compensation is a vexed question. There can be no golden rule applicable to all cases for measuring the value of human life or a limb. Measure of damages cannot be arrived at by precise mathematical calculations. It would depend upon the particular facts and circumstances, and attending peculiar or special features, if any. Every method or mode adopted for assessing compensation has to be considered in the background of "just" compensation which is the pivotal consideration. Though by use of the expression "which appears to it to be just", a wide discretion is vested in the Tribunal,
the determination has to be rational, to be done MACT No .348/2018 Vineet Shaky vs. Amir Page No. 13 of 27 by a judicious approach and not the outcome of whims,
wild guesses and arbitrariness.. ..." 
30. Delineating the damages as pecuniary and non pecuniary, Hon'ble Supreme Court of India, in case of R. D. Hattangadi Vs. Pest Control (India) Pvt Ltd, 1995 AIR 755, made following observations: 
"9....while fixing an amount of compensation payable to a victim of an accident, the damages have to be assessed separately as pecuniary damages and special damages. 
Pecuniary damages are those which the victim has actually incurred and which are capable of being calculated in terms of money; whereas non-pecuniary damages are those which are incapable of being assessed by arithmetical calculations. In order to appreciate two concepts pecuniary damages may include expenses incurred by the claimant: (i) medical attendance; (ii) loss of earning of profit up to the date of trial;
(iii) other material loss. So far non- pecuniary damages are concerned, they may include (i) damages for mental and physical shock, pain and suffering, already suffered or likely to be suffered in future; (ii) damages to compensate for the loss of amenities of life which may include a variety of matters i.e. on account of injury the claimant may not be able to walk, run or sit; (iii) damages for the loss of expectation of life, i.e., on account of injury the normal longevity of the person concerned is shortened; (iv) inconvenience, hardship, discomfort, disappointment, frustration and mental stress in life."

8 31. Certain principles for delineating just compensation were enumerated in the case of Raj Kumar Vs. Ajay Kumar & Anr., (2011) 1 SCC 343, by Hon'ble Supreme Court of India. Following observations are relevant in the context:
"40.General principles relating to compensation in injury cases MACT No .348/2018 Vineet Shaky vs. Amir Page No. 14 of 27 5. The provision of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 ("the Act", for short) makes it clear that the award must be just, which means that compensation should, to the extent possible, fully and adequately restore the claimant to the position prior to the accident. The object of awarding damages is to make good the loss suffered as a result of wrong done as far as money can do so, in a fair, reasonable and equitable manner. 
The court or the Tribunal shall have to assess the damages objectively and exclude from consideration any speculation or fancy, though some conjecture with reference to the nature of disability and its consequences, is inevitable. A person is not only to be compensated for the physical injury, but also for the loss which he suffered as a result of such injury. This means that he is to be compensated for his inability to lead a full life, his inability to enjoy those normal amenities which he would have enjoyed but for the injuries, and his inability to earn as much as he used to earn or could have earned. [See C.K. Subramania Iyer v. T. Kunhikuttan Nair [(1969) 3 SCC 64 : AIR 1970 SC 376] , R.D. Hattangadi v. Pest Control (India) (P) Ltd. [(1995) 1 SCC 551 :
1995 SCC (Cri) 250] and Baker v. Willoughby [1970 AC 467 : (1970) 2 WLR 50 :
(1969) 3 All ER 1528 (HL)] .] 
6. The heads under which compensation is awarded in personal injury cases are the following:
Pecuniary damages (Special damages)
(i) Expenses relating to treatment, hospitalisation, medicines, transportation,
nourishing food, and miscellaneous expenditure. 
(ii) Loss of earnings (and other gains) which the injured would have made had he not been injured, comprising:
(a) Loss of earning during the period of treatment;
(b) Loss of future earnings on account of permanent disability.
(iii) Future medical expenses.
Non-pecuniary damages (General damages) MACT No .348/2018 Vineet Shaky vs. Amir Page No. 15 of 27 Vineet Shaky vs Amir on 4 July, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/27361723/
9 (iv) Damages for pain, suffering and trauma as a consequence of the injuries. 
(v) Loss of amenities (and/or loss of prospects of marriage). 
(vi) Loss of expectation of life (shortening of normal longevity). In routine personal injury cases,
compensation will be awarded only under heads (i), (ii)(a) and (iv). It is only in serious cases of injury, where there is specific medical evidence corroborating the evidence of the claimant, that compensation will be granted under any of the heads (ii)(b), (iii), (v) and (vi) relating to loss of future earnings on account of permanent disability, future medical expenses, loss of amenities (and/or loss of prospects of marriage) and loss of expectation of life.
7. Assessment of pecuniary damages under Item (i) and under Item (ii)
(a) do not pose much difficulty as they involve reimbursement of actuals and are easily ascertainable from the evidence. Award under the head of future medical expenses--Item (iii)--depends upon specific medical evidence regarding need for further treatment and cost thereof. Assessment of non-pecuniary damages--Items (iv), (v) and (vi)-- involves determination of lump sum amounts with reference to circumstances such as age, nature of injury/deprivation/ disability suffered by the claimant and the effect thereof on the future life of the claimant. Decisions of this Court and the High Courts contain necessary guidelines for award under these heads, if necessary. What usually poses some difficulty is the assessment of the loss of future earnings on account of permanent disability--Item (ii)(a). We are concerned with that assessment in this case." 
32. It is settled proposition of law as held in catena of judgments that "just compensation" should include all elements that would go to place the victim in as near a position as she or he was in, before the occurrence of the accident. Whilst no amount of money or other material compensation can erase the trauma, pain and MACT No .348/2018 Vineet Shaky vs. Amir Page No. 16 of 27 suffering that a victim undergoes after a serious accident, (or replace the loss of a loved one), monetary compensation is the manner known to law, whereby society assures some measure of restitution to those who survive, and the victims who have to face their lives. 
33. PW1/Claimant has deposed that he was employed as Salesman with Paramount Road Safety Equipment Pvt. Ltd, Jasola, Delhi and was drawing monthly salary of Rs.15,000/-. To prove his employment, claimant also summoned Sh. Nitin Kumar Saxena, Manager of the said company as PW2, who produced copy of letter of appointment of claimant and salary slips running from April 2016 to September 2017 coupled with payment record of the company. It is thus accepted that claimant was employed upon monthly salary of Rs.15,000/-. Considering that the injuries sustained were grievous in nature, for which he remained hospitalized in total 12-13 days, though no leave record has been filed, presumably as injuries would have taken considerable time to get healed, loss of income for four months is being granted.

Ltd., MAC Appeal no. 433/2013, decided on 18.10.2022 it was noted regarding rate of interest:
"25 to evaluate the submission made by counsel for the applicants, it is imperative to examine the guiding principles for the grant of interest.
MACT No .348/2018 Vineet Shaky vs. Amir Page No. 19 of 27 In Abati Bezbaruah Vs.
Geological Survey of India, (2003) 3 SCC 148, the following was held while interpreting section 171 of the MV Act, 1988:-
Three decisions were cited before us by Mr. A. P. Mohanty, learned counsel appearing on behalf of the Appellant, in support of his contentions.
